To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the BRCA1 gene is associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancers.
the BRCA1 gene is mutated in 5-10% of breast cancer patients, and that the majority of these mutations are founder effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the BRCA1 gene and the characterization of the mutations in the gene that are associated with breast cancer.
the development of new methods to detect mutations in the BRCA1 gene.
the development of a new technique for the detection of BRCA1 mutations and the application of this method to the study of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BRCA1 mutations account for approximately 20–40% of hereditary breast cancer and ∼80–90% of hereditary ovarian cancers.

the BRCA1 gene is associated with a high risk of breast and ovarian cancers in women, and that the risk of breast and/or ovarian cancer is higher in women carrying the BRCA1 mutations than in the general population.
the BRCA1 gene is a tumor suppressor gene that plays an important role in cell cycle control.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BRCA1 gene has 24 exons, and the BRCA1 protein contains 1863 amino acids with a molecular mass of 220 kD (2,3).
the BRCA1 gene is the most common gene to be mutated in familial breast cancer.
the BRCA1 gene is a complex, highly polymorphic, and large gene, with many mutations, and the detection of these mutations is a difficult task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes play an important role in the development of breast cancer.
